edits.after: A gram of radium then sold for one hundred thousand dollars. The process for preparing it had been published years earlier, without reserve, by Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie, and the radium industry was now thriving on that very process and selling its product at a high price. She had helped give the method away, yet the radium in her laboratory was used at that time only for extracting emanations for hospital use, and Meloney, who later wrote the book's introduction, set out to raise a subscription in America to enable her to go on with her work. In her book she worked through that account line by line.

edits.before: The story begins in Paris in the late 1890s. The Curies wanted to purify a new radioactive substance far enough to be sure it was a new element, and they lacked a proper place to work in, personnel and money. Pitchblende was an expensive mineral, and they could not afford to buy a sufficient quantity. At that time the principal source of this mineral was at St. Joachimsthal in Bohemia, where the Austrian government worked a mine for the extraction of uranium. Its residues had so far not been used at all, and they believed the radium, and part of the polonium, would be found in them. Through the influence of the Vienna Academy of Sciences they secured several tons of the residues at an advantageous price. In the beginning the costs came out of their own pockets; only later were they given a few subventions and some help from outside sources.

edits.before: The new post came without a laboratory. In the annex at 12 rue Cuvier that served as teaching quarters for the P.C.N., all he had at his disposition was a little office and a single work room. He meant to receive students and start them in research, so he took steps to find larger working quarters. Anyone who has taken similar steps knows the wall of financial and administrative obstacles he was throwing himself against: the official letters, the visits, the requests, and what even the least success entailed. It all thoroughly wearied and discouraged him. Meanwhile the research could not advance without industrial means of treating the raw material. In 1899 Pierre Curie organized a first industrial experiment, using for it a chance installation placed at his disposition by the Central Society of Chemical Products, with which he had dealt over the construction of his balances. The technical details were arranged very successfully by André Debierne, and the operations brought good results, though a special crew had to be trained for chemical work that demanded special precautions.
